items.prompt: A company must back up all production databases and volumes, but must exclude development resources and assign different retention policies by environment. Which design is most maintainable?
constraints: Resources are tagged consistently.
AWS Backup supports the selected resource types.
Coverage must be auditable.

options.text: Create AWS Backup plans and resource selections that use approved tags or explicit resource lists, then monitor that tagged production resources are covered and development resources are excluded.
Create one security group per backup plan because AWS Backup selects resources from network membership.
Use CloudTrail event selectors because they automatically create backups for resources that emit management events.
Back up every resource with one global plan and rely on owners to delete development recovery points later.

feedback.Reason: AWS Backup resource selections can use tags or explicit resources, allowing policy-driven coverage and class-specific plans.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup plans define schedules and lifecycle, while resource assignments determine which supported resources receive the plan. Tags require governance and validation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform enforces required environment and backup-policy tags, reports unassigned production resources, and tests an excluded development resource.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups do not select backup resources, CloudTrail records events rather than creating backups, and one global plan does not express environment-specific retention safely.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tag-based assignment scales better but fails silently if tags drift, so coverage evidence and deny-by-default onboarding checks are needed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security-group membership is a network concept and is not the AWS Backup resource-selection model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudTrail event selectors control recorded events and do not create resource backups.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A global plan can over-retain or under-protect classes and leaves dangerous manual cleanup for development data.

items.prompt: A supported workload needs a recovery point that can be selected continuously rather than only at a daily schedule. Which AWS Backup capability should be evaluated first?
constraints: The resource type supports continuous backup.
The recovery window is defined by the service.
The team must verify restore behavior.

options.text: Use an AWS Backup plan rule that enables continuous backup for the supported resource, then verify the available recovery window and test a restore.
Use a weekly snapshot because a scheduled snapshot always provides a continuous recovery point.
Use S3 Cross-Region Replication because replication automatically creates point-in-time backup history for every service.
Use an IAM policy condition because policy evaluation stores every prior resource state.

feedback.Reason: AWS Backup continuous backup, where supported, is the service capability intended to provide a continuously maintained recovery point within a defined window.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Continuous backup is a resource- and Region-dependent AWS Backup feature. It has a supported recovery window and is distinct from periodic snapshot rules.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks feature availability for the resource, configures the rule, and validates that the restore point selection and recovery process meet the workload objective.
Details.errorCorrection: A weekly snapshot has scheduled granularity, S3 replication does not back up arbitrary services, and IAM policies do not store resource history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Continuous recovery can improve recovery-point precision but is not universal and must be weighed against service support, cost, and restore characteristics.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A weekly snapshot provides periodic recovery points and cannot represent continuous recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 replication applies to S3 objects and is not a general backup mechanism for other AWS resources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM policy evaluation authorizes requests and does not retain resource-state history.

items.prompt: An RDS database requires a manually controlled recovery copy in another Region for disaster recovery. Which approach provides that copy?
constraints: The target Region may be unavailable during a regional event.
The copy must be independently retained.
Encryption and ownership must be planned.

options.text: Create or select an RDS automated or manual snapshot according to the objective and copy it to the target Region, configuring the destination encryption and retention controls.
Enable Multi-AZ in the source Region because a synchronous standby is always a cross-Region disaster-recovery copy.
Use a read-only IAM policy because authorization replication creates an independent database snapshot in another Region.
Use an S3 lifecycle transition because RDS snapshots are objects that can be moved between S3 storage classes by the customer.

feedback.Reason: RDS snapshot copy creates a separately managed snapshot in another Region and is a direct building block for regional recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: RDS supports copying snapshots across Regions, with destination encryption and snapshot permissions considered independently of the source.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery owner schedules or triggers cross-Region copies, verifies the destination key and account policy, and rehearses restoring a database in the target Region.
Details.errorCorrection: Multi-AZ is an in-Region availability design, IAM policies do not replicate data, and customers do not lifecycle RDS snapshots through S3.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-Region copies improve regional recovery but add copy time, storage, transfer, key, and operational cutover costs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Multi-AZ provides high availability within the configured Region and is not an independent cross-Region snapshot.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM policy replication changes authorization, not database data or snapshot state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: RDS snapshots are managed by RDS and are not customer-managed S3 objects for lifecycle transitions.

items.prompt: A design review proposes Multi-AZ as the only protection against accidental deletion of an RDS database. What correction is needed?
constraints: The workload needs instance failover.
Users can make destructive changes.
Historical recovery is also required.

options.text: Use Multi-AZ for high availability and failover, but retain automated backups or snapshots for point-in-time and historical recovery.
Use Multi-AZ alone because the standby always preserves every deleted row as a restorable historical version.
Disable backups because a second Availability Zone makes deletion impossible at the database layer.
Use an IAM permissions boundary because it converts a standby instance into a backup repository.

feedback.Reason: Multi-AZ improves availability and failover, while backups provide historical recovery from corruption or deletion.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A Multi-AZ standby is part of the database availability architecture and is not a user-accessible historical backup. Automated backups and snapshots serve recovery objectives.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect documents separate HA and data-recovery controls, validates failover, and tests restoring a prior database state.
Details.errorCorrection: A standby does not create historical row versions, deletion can propagate to the active database, and IAM boundaries do not store database data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Using both controls costs more than either alone but addresses different failure classes and should be evaluated against RTO and RPO.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Multi-AZ failover is not a historical restore mechanism for deleted or corrupted data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A standby does not make destructive database changes impossible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Permissions boundaries constrain IAM roles and do not create backup repositories.

items.prompt: A globally distributed application needs low-latency reads and writes in multiple Regions, with managed replication between regional table replicas. Which service capability fits?
constraints: The workload is DynamoDB-based.
Applications write in more than one Region.
Conflict and consistency behavior must be designed.

options.text: Evaluate DynamoDB Global Tables, including its multi-Region replication model, conflict behavior, capacity, and operational recovery requirements.
Use DynamoDB Streams alone because a stream automatically exposes a writable table replica in every Region.
Use an RDS Multi-AZ standby because it creates DynamoDB replicas without application changes.
Use S3 Cross-Region Replication because DynamoDB tables are stored as S3 objects behind the service.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB Global Tables provide managed multi-Region, multi-active table replication for supported workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Global Tables create replicas in multiple Regions and replicate item changes; the chosen version, conflict resolution, capacity, and failover model must match the workload.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team models write ownership and conflicts, provisions replicas, monitors replication health, and tests regional failover and recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Streams are an event source rather than a managed writable replica, RDS Multi-AZ applies to RDS, and S3 replication does not copy DynamoDB tables.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Global Tables improve regional latency and availability but add multi-Region cost, conflict resolution, and consistency design complexity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: DynamoDB Streams expose item changes but do not by themselves create managed writable table replicas.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RDS Multi-AZ is an RDS feature and cannot replicate DynamoDB tables.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 replication applies to S3 objects and does not replicate DynamoDB table data.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB table needs an application-triggered full backup before a risky migration, independent of the table’s point-in-time recovery setting. Which operation should be used?
constraints: The backup must be a complete table backup.
The migration team controls the trigger.
The backup should not interrupt normal table access.

options.text: Create an on-demand DynamoDB backup before the migration, protect its access, and verify how it will be restored into a new table if required.
Enable a DynamoDB stream because each stream record is a complete immutable copy of the table at migration time.
Use a security group snapshot because DynamoDB backup contents are represented by network state.
Delete and recreate the table because a fresh table is the only supported DynamoDB backup operation.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB on-demand backup creates a full table backup that can be initiated independently of the continuous PITR setting.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: On-demand backups create a restorable backup without consuming table read capacity or requiring application downtime, subject to service behavior and permissions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The migration runbook creates and verifies the backup, restricts deletion, and rehearses restoring it into an isolated table before the production change.
Details.errorCorrection: Streams contain change records rather than a guaranteed full table backup, security groups do not represent DynamoDB data, and recreation destroys rather than preserves state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: On-demand backups provide explicit recovery points but add storage and lifecycle management that must be governed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A stream is a change feed and is not the direct full-table backup operation described.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DynamoDB backup data is not represented by a security-group snapshot.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting and recreating a table is destructive and is not a backup strategy.

items.prompt: Objects written to a source S3 bucket must be copied automatically to a bucket in another Region for regional access and continuity. Which control should be configured?
constraints: The source and destination buckets are versioned.
The destination is in another Region.
The replication role and destination ownership must be governed.

options.text: Configure an S3 Cross-Region Replication rule with the required source filter, destination, IAM role, encryption handling, and ownership or access settings.
Use S3 Lifecycle transition because lifecycle rules copy every object to a bucket in another Region.
Use an RDS snapshot copy because S3 buckets are represented as relational database snapshots.
Use a VPC route table because S3 replication follows the route table of the source bucket.

feedback.Reason: S3 Replication is the managed object-level mechanism for asynchronously copying selected source objects to a destination bucket, including across Regions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replication requires versioning and a rule with source scope, destination, and permissions. Replication status and failure handling must be monitored.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests new and existing object behavior, validates destination encryption and ownership, and measures replication lag before relying on the copy.
Details.errorCorrection: Lifecycle changes storage state in a bucket, RDS snapshots apply to databases, and S3 replication is not controlled by VPC route tables.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replication improves regional availability and distribution but is asynchronous and does not replace a point-in-time backup or protection from logical corruption.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: S3 Lifecycle transitions objects between storage classes and does not copy them to another bucket.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RDS snapshot copy does not operate on S3 buckets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 service replication rules are not selected through VPC route tables.

items.prompt: A team assumes that deleting an object in the source bucket automatically deletes the replica, but the destination must preserve recovery copies from accidental deletes. What should be configured and verified?
constraints: The buckets use Versioning.
Accidental source deletes are possible.
The destination is a recovery copy, not a mirror that must delete immediately.

options.text: Review the S3 replication delete-marker and version-deletion behavior, configure the rule and delete-marker replication deliberately, and test source-delete recovery in the destination.
Assume replication always mirrors every delete because replicas are exactly the same object history without configuration.
Disable Versioning because delete markers are the only reason replication cannot copy objects across Regions.
Use an IAM Allow on DeleteObject in the source because an Allow makes the destination immune to source deletions.

feedback.Reason: S3 replication behavior for delete markers and version deletes is a policy decision that must be tested against whether the destination is a mirror or a recovery copy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Versioning and replication configuration determine how object versions, delete markers, and explicit version deletions are handled; behavior is not safely inferred from a simple mirror assumption.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery owner tests accidental delete, intentional version delete, and restore procedures before calling the destination a recovery copy.
Details.errorCorrection: Replication does not imply every delete is propagated identically, disabling Versioning undermines the model, and IAM Allow does not protect a destination.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Preserving destination history improves recovery but can increase storage and complicate cleanup; deletion policy must be explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Delete propagation depends on the replication configuration and object-version behavior; it must not be assumed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 replication requires Versioning and does not become safer by disabling it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An Allow to delete the source does not make the destination immune to replicated deletion behavior.

items.prompt: Encrypted S3 objects must replicate to another account and Region using a customer managed KMS key in the destination. Which dependency must the architect include?
constraints: Source and destination accounts differ.
The objects use SSE-KMS.
The destination key is controlled by the destination security team.

options.text: Configure S3 replication with the required source and destination permissions, allow the replication role to use the destination KMS key, and validate the key policy and bucket policy together.
Grant the source workload unrestricted kms:* because any source principal automatically becomes a destination key administrator.
Use SSE-S3 for the destination without reviewing requirements because encryption mode is irrelevant to replication authorization.
Use a security group on the KMS key because network access alone grants S3 replication permission to encrypt objects.

feedback.Reason: SSE-KMS replication requires an end-to-end authorization path involving the replication role, source and destination S3 policies, and the destination KMS key policy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The replication service must be allowed to decrypt or use source data as required and encrypt with the destination KMS key. Cross-account key policy and IAM permissions must align.
Details.scenarioApplication: Security grants only the replication role the needed key actions, tests a replicated object, and monitors failures caused by policy or key changes.
Details.errorCorrection: The source workload need not be a key administrator, encryption mode affects the authorization path, and KMS keys do not use security groups as permissions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer managed keys improve ownership and auditability but add cross-account policy and lifecycle dependencies that can break replication.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replication should use a scoped service role and key permissions, not unrestricted source workload administration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The selected encryption mode changes the required replication authorization and cannot be ignored.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: KMS authorization is policy-based; security groups do not grant key use.

items.prompt: An EFS file system must be included in the organization’s centralized backup policy with the same retention evidence as other supported resources. Which approach is appropriate?
constraints: The file system is in a supported Region.
The organization uses AWS Backup centrally.
Restore validation is required.

options.text: Assign the EFS file system to an AWS Backup plan, configure its lifecycle and vault, and test restoring the file system or supported recovery point into an isolated target.
Use EFS lifecycle management because moving files to an infrequent-access class creates an independent backup copy.
Use a route table association because EFS backup coverage is determined by the subnet route table.
Use a read-only mount target because a mount target is a point-in-time copy of the file system.

feedback.Reason: AWS Backup can centralize supported EFS protection under a backup plan and vault with common governance.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The backup plan controls schedule and lifecycle; the vault controls backup storage and access. Coverage and restore support must be verified for the deployment.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks plan assignment, backup job success, vault retention, and a restore into a separate file system before declaring compliance.
Details.errorCorrection: EFS lifecycle changes storage class within the same file system, routes do not select backups, and mount targets provide access rather than copies.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Centralized backup improves policy consistency but still requires file-system capacity, permissions, mount, and restore testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Lifecycle transitions optimize file storage and do not create an independent backup recovery point.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route tables do not determine AWS Backup coverage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A mount target is a network access point and is not a point-in-time file-system copy.

items.prompt: The platform team wants an FSx file system protected by the same central vault and backup policy as its other application resources. What should be checked before implementation?
constraints: The FSx file-system type is known.
The central vault has defined retention.
Native and centralized backup capabilities may differ.

options.text: Check the FSx type and Region against AWS Backup support, then choose native automatic backups, AWS Backup, or both according to the required recovery points and governance evidence.
Assume every FSx type has identical backup features and configure the first plan without checking support.
Use S3 replication because FSx backup support is implemented as an S3 bucket policy.
Use Multi-AZ networking as a substitute for historical FSx recovery points.

feedback.Reason: FSx backup choices depend on the file-system type and supported integration; the architect must verify the actual capability before selecting a control.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: FSx has service-specific native backup behavior, and AWS Backup support varies by resource type and Region. The chosen path must match retention and restore needs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team confirms support, maps native backups and centralized vault copies, and runs a restore test using the same operational identity expected during an incident.
Details.errorCorrection: FSx types are not interchangeable, S3 replication does not back up FSx, and network redundancy does not create historical recovery points.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Using both native and centralized copies may increase cost but can separate fast operational recovery from governed long-term recovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Backup capability is resource-type and Region dependent and must be verified.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 replication is an object-replication feature and is not the FSx backup policy.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network or deployment redundancy does not provide historical backup points.

items.prompt: A workload’s EBS volumes need encrypted recovery copies in another account and Region. Which sequence is required?
constraints: The destination account owns the recovery boundary.
The snapshots are encrypted.
The destination team controls the destination KMS key.

options.text: Share or copy the EBS snapshot according to the supported cross-account process, grant the required KMS permissions, and create an encrypted destination snapshot owned by the recovery account.
Copy the volume’s security group because a security-group copy includes the encrypted EBS blocks and KMS metadata.
Use an IAM role without any KMS or snapshot permissions because encryption is transparent to all accounts.
Replicate the EC2 instance ID to the other Region because an instance identifier is a complete volume recovery point.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account encrypted EBS snapshot recovery requires coordinated snapshot sharing or copying and KMS authorization in the source and destination boundaries.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An encrypted snapshot copy must be authorized through EBS and KMS policies. The destination account should own the copied snapshot so the recovery boundary is independent.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery account tests copying and creating a volume, verifies key access, and protects the destination snapshot from source-account compromise.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups contain network rules, encryption does not remove authorization requirements, and an EC2 instance ID is not volume data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent snapshot ownership improves isolation but adds cross-account KMS governance and copy time or transfer cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security groups do not contain EBS volume blocks or snapshot data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cross-account encrypted snapshot operations require the relevant EBS and KMS permissions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An instance identifier does not reproduce the contents or state of an EBS volume.

items.prompt: A Redis-compatible ElastiCache workload needs a restorable copy before a schema migration, while the cache remains disposable during normal operation. Which control fits?
constraints: The cache data can be reconstructed but migration rollback is needed.
A point-in-time snapshot is sufficient.
The snapshot must be protected and tested.

options.text: Create an ElastiCache snapshot before the migration, apply the service’s snapshot retention and access controls, and test restoring into an isolated replication group.
Use a security group rule because cache snapshots are recreated from allowed client IP addresses.
Use S3 Object Lock directly on the cache node because every Redis key is an S3 object version.
Rely on cache eviction metrics because a metric can recreate the exact pre-migration key values.

feedback.Reason: ElastiCache snapshots provide a service-native point-in-time copy for supported engines and restore workflows.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ElastiCache snapshots capture cache data for backup or migration and can be used to create a new replication group; network controls do not create snapshots.
Details.scenarioApplication: The migration runbook takes a snapshot, verifies its status, restores a test group, and retains or deletes it according to the rollback window.
Details.errorCorrection: Security groups only control access, S3 Object Lock does not apply to cache keys, and metrics cannot reconstruct data values.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Snapshots add storage and snapshot-time cost but may provide a useful rollback point even when the cache is normally rebuildable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Client network rules do not create or contain ElastiCache snapshot data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: ElastiCache data is not governed by attaching S3 Object Lock to a cache node.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Metrics describe behavior and do not contain the exact key-value dataset.

items.prompt: A Redshift data warehouse needs a recovery copy retained beyond the cluster’s normal automated snapshot window and available in another Region. Which design should be used?
constraints: The data warehouse is a provisioned or supported Redshift cluster.
Long-term retention is required.
Regional recovery must be tested.

options.text: Configure Redshift automated or manual snapshots as appropriate, set retention, and copy snapshots to the target Region or account according to the recovery design.
Use an EC2 AMI because a Redshift cluster is restored by launching the same instance image.
Use a VPC endpoint policy because endpoint policies store historical warehouse blocks for regional recovery.
Disable snapshots and rely only on database connection logs because SQL statements are sufficient to reconstruct all warehouse state.

feedback.Reason: Redshift snapshots and snapshot copies are the service-native recovery artifacts for a warehouse cluster.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Redshift supports automated and manual snapshots with retention and copy options. A destination copy must be restored and validated in the target Region.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team defines snapshot retention, protects the snapshot permissions and key, copies it to the recovery Region, and rehearses cluster restore.
Details.errorCorrection: EC2 AMIs do not contain Redshift cluster state, endpoint policies govern service access, and connection logs do not reconstruct warehouse data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Snapshot copies support regional recovery but add storage, transfer, restore time, and compatibility considerations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An EC2 AMI is not a Redshift cluster snapshot.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: VPC endpoint policies do not store Redshift data or create recovery points.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Connection logs cannot reconstruct the full warehouse state.

items.prompt: A team reports successful backup jobs but has never restored a recovery point. What is the most important next action before declaring the control effective?
constraints: The recovery point exists.
The restore target can be isolated.
The result must be evidence for an audit and an incident runbook.

options.text: Perform a controlled restore into an isolated target, validate data integrity and application behavior, measure RTO, and record the result and follow-up actions.
Check only the backup job status because a successful job guarantees an application-consistent restore.
Increase the backup frequency without restoring because more recovery points remove the need for restore testing.
Delete the recovery point after checking its metadata because deletion proves the backup can be recreated.

feedback.Reason: A backup is operationally useful only when it can be restored and the restored system meets integrity and recovery objectives.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Restore testing validates permissions, keys, dependencies, application consistency, data integrity, and recovery time, not merely backup-job completion.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team restores in isolation, runs application checks, measures RTO, documents defects, and repeats after material architecture or policy changes.
Details.errorCorrection: A successful job can still produce an unusable restore, more frequency does not prove usability, and deletion is not a restore test.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Restore testing consumes time and resources but is the evidence that turns configured backups into a credible recovery capability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Job success confirms backup execution but not application-consistent restore or recovery time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More recovery points do not validate permissions, dependencies, integrity, or restore procedure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting a recovery point is destructive and does not demonstrate recoverability.

items.prompt: A database is asynchronously replicated to another Region, but an operator can accidentally delete data in the primary. What additional control is needed for historical recovery?
constraints: Replication may propagate writes and deletes.
The business requires recovery before the mistake.
The second Region is also part of the production path.

options.text: Add independently retained backups or snapshots with a recovery window, because replication improves availability but does not by itself protect against logical corruption or propagated deletion.
Remove all replication because backups and replication cannot coexist in one architecture.
Increase replica read capacity because more read capacity creates historical versions of deleted data.
Use a public endpoint so an operator can recover the deleted data from the network path.

feedback.Reason: Replication and backup address different failure models; a separately retained recovery point is needed when logical errors can propagate.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Replication keeps another copy current or near-current, while backups preserve historical states that can be selected after corruption, deletion, or operator error.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect keeps replication for regional continuity and adds protected backups with restore testing and a controlled recovery procedure.
Details.errorCorrection: The controls can coexist, read capacity does not create history, and public exposure is not a recovery mechanism.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Two controls cost more and need coordinated failover and restore decisions, but they cover distinct availability and data-recovery risks.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Replication and backup serve different objectives and can be used together.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Read capacity changes performance and does not preserve historical deleted data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A public endpoint changes reachability and cannot recover a prior data state.

items.prompt: Backups must remain recoverable if the production account is compromised, and the recovery account owns the encryption key. Which ownership model is strongest?
constraints: The backup copy is in a separate account.
The destination key is customer managed.
Production administrators must not be able to delete the recovery key.

options.text: Use a destination recovery account and vault with a customer managed KMS key owned and governed there, grant only required backup-service and restore roles, and test key-dependent recovery.
Use the production account’s root credentials as the permanent key owner because root is the only identity that can restore backups.
Use a security group to protect the KMS key because backup encryption is controlled by the network path.
Delete the destination KMS key after each backup because a deleted key makes encrypted recovery inaccessible to attackers but still restorable by AWS.

feedback.Reason: Independent destination ownership of the backup vault and encryption key reduces dependence on the compromised production account.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backup recovery requires the vault, recovery point, IAM permissions, and KMS key to remain usable. A separate account and key policy create an independent control boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The recovery team limits production access, tests restore with the destination role, and documents key rotation and emergency access without using root as a workload identity.
Details.errorCorrection: Root is not the only restore identity, network groups do not protect keys, and deleting a key destroys the ability to decrypt the backup.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent key ownership improves isolation but increases cross-account policy, monitoring, and key-lifecycle responsibilities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Root credentials should not be a permanent workload or recovery mechanism, and restore permissions can be delegated.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: KMS keys use key and IAM policies, not security groups, for authorization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting the key would make the encrypted recovery point unusable rather than safely recoverable.

items.prompt: An audit dashboard reports only the number of successful backup jobs, but production resources can be launched without backup tags. What must be added?
constraints: Backup policies are tag-based.
A job can succeed while another resource is unprotected.
Security needs actionable evidence.

options.text: Monitor both backup-job outcomes and resource coverage: detect unassigned or noncompliant production resources, alert on failed jobs, and retain evidence of recovery-point and restore tests.
Track only total successful jobs because a successful job proves every production resource is protected.
Disable tagging and back up only resources that operators remember to select during incidents.
Use a public S3 inventory as proof because inventory lists every AWS resource regardless of backup assignment.

feedback.Reason: Effective backup governance measures coverage and recovery outcomes, not just successful jobs for resources that happened to be assigned.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A backup control has at least discovery or coverage, execution, retention, restore, and evidence dimensions. Tag drift can create an unprotected resource without a failed job.
Details.scenarioApplication: The organization reconciles inventory to backup assignments, alerts on gaps, records failed jobs, and reports restore-test results to owners.
Details.errorCorrection: Job counts do not prove coverage, manual incident selection is unreliable, and S3 Inventory does not enumerate arbitrary AWS resources or backup assignment.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Coverage monitoring adds integration and ownership work but closes the gap between configured policy and actual protected assets.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A successful job can coexist with an unassigned production resource and therefore does not prove coverage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Manual selection during an incident is too late and creates an avoidable protection gap.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 Inventory is limited to S3 objects and is not evidence of account-wide backup coverage.
